title: Statistical Tests and Analysis
text:
This section covers common statistical tests used in medical research, implemented in R.



# Load necessary libraries
library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.4     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(gtsummary)

# Example data (simulated; the seed makes the numbers the same on every render)
set.seed(2026)
data <- data.frame(
  age = rnorm(100, 50, 10),
  blood_pressure = rnorm(100, 120, 15),
  treatment = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE)
)

# Summary statistics
data %>% 
  tbl_summary()

# Two-sample t-test
t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = 1.0107, df = 96.367, p-value = 0.3147
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.804691  8.624570
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       123.3066        120.3966 






# Create categorical data
data$outcome <- sample(c("Improved", "Not Improved"), 100, replace = TRUE)

# Chi-square test
chisq.test(table(data$treatment, data$outcome))


    Pearson's Chi-squared test with Yates' continuity correction

data:  table(data$treatment, data$outcome)
X-squared = 1.0283, df = 1, p-value = 0.3106

t.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
t = 1.0107, df = 96.367, p-value = 0.3147
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group A and group B is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -2.804691  8.624570
sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       123.3066        120.3966 



R uses Welch’s t-test by default (does not assume equal variances).
The confidence interval is for the first group minus the second (A − B), so the sign follows the order of the groups.
The sample estimates show each group’s mean.





# paired: the same 30 people before and after
before <- rnorm(30, 140, 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, 5, 6)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 5.3735, df = 29, p-value = 8.985e-06
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 3.020140 6.731862
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       4.876001 

# non-parametric alternative for two independent groups
wilcox.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
W = 1360, p-value = 0.4482
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0






A p-value says how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result is “due to chance”.
It says nothing about the size or importance of the difference: look at the estimate and its confidence interval.
A large p-value is weak evidence against “no difference”. It is not proof that there is none.





Regression modeling now has its own dedicated module — see Regression Analysis for simple/multiple regression, diagnostics, and logistic regression.

title: Merging Datasets
text:
This module explains how to combine datasets by rows, columns, and with joins.



data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"), Age = c(23, 35, 28))
data2 <- data.frame(ID = 4:6, Name = c("David", "Eva", "Frank"), Age = c(45, 30, 40))
merged_rows <- rbind(data1, data2)
merged_rows

  ID    Name Age
1  1   Alice  23
2  2     Bob  35
3  3 Charlie  28
4  4   David  45
5  5     Eva  30
6  6   Frank  40






data1 <- data.frame(ID = 1:3, Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"))
data2 <- data.frame(Age = c(23, 35, 28), Height = c(165, 180, 175))
merged_columns <- cbind(data1, data2)
merged_columns

  ID    Name Age Height
1  1   Alice  23    165
2  2     Bob  35    180
3  3 Charlie  28    175






library(dplyr)


Attaching package: 'dplyr'


The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':

    filter, lag


The following objects are masked from 'package:base':

    intersect, setdiff, setequal, union

data1 <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva")
)
data2 <- data.frame(
  ID = c(2, 3, 5, 6),
  Score = c(85, 90, 88, 92)
)

inner_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88

left_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88

right_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  2     Bob    85
2  3 Charlie    90
3  5     Eva    88
4  6    <NA>    92

full_join(data1, data2, by = "ID")

  ID    Name Score
1  1   Alice    NA
2  2     Bob    85
3  3 Charlie    90
4  4   David    NA
5  5     Eva    88
6  6    <NA>    92


These join types are useful for combining medical records, survey forms, and measurement datasets.



bind_rows() (dplyr) does the same job as rbind(): tables with the same columns, different people.

library(dplyr)
round1 <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(120, 135, 142))
round2 <- data.frame(id = 4:6, sbp = c(128, 150, 118))
bind_rows(round1, round2)

  id sbp
1  1 120
2  2 135
3  3 142
4  4 128
5  5 150
6  6 118





cbind() pastes by position and never checks who is who. If the two tables are sorted differently, the columns are silently mixed up. Join by a key such as id instead.




patients <- data.frame(id = 1:5, name = c("Asha", "Bina", "Chetan", "Dev", "Esha"))
labs     <- data.frame(id = c(3, 3, 5), hba1c = c(7.1, 6.8, 8.0))   # id 3 was tested twice
nrow(patients)

[1] 5

nrow(left_join(patients, labs, by = "id"))   # 6: patient 3 appears twice

[1] 6

count(labs, id)                                # check the key before joining

  id n
1  3 2
2  5 1


A left join keeps every patient, but a patient who matches two lab rows appears twice. Count rows before and after every join, and check that the key is unique in the table you join to.



The same blood pressures can be stored wide (one row per person, one column per measurement) or long (one row per person and measurement). ggplot2 and most models want long data.

library(tidyr)
wide <- data.frame(id = 1:3, sbp = c(128, 142, 135), dbp = c(82, 90, 85))
long <- pivot_longer(wide, cols = c(sbp, dbp), names_to = "measure", values_to = "mmHg")
long

# A tibble: 6 × 3
     id measure  mmHg
  <int> <chr>   <dbl>
1     1 sbp       128
2     1 dbp        82
3     2 sbp       142
4     2 dbp        90
5     3 sbp       135
6     3 dbp        85

pivot_wider(long, names_from = measure, values_from = mmHg)   # and back again

# A tibble: 3 × 3
     id   sbp   dbp
  <int> <dbl> <dbl>
1     1   128    82
2     2   142    90
3     3   135    85


pivot_longer() never changes the number of values: 3 people × 2 measurements = 6 rows.

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
How to Read Box Plots
Using the previous plot:

Reading the 5-Number Summary (Control / Intervention): - Bottom whisker: lowest value within 1.5 × IQR of the box - Bottom of box (Q1): 25th percentile (22.4 / 23.0) - Line in box (Median): 50th percentile (24.6 / 25.8) - Top of box (Q3): 75th percentile (27.7 / 29.3) - Top whisker: highest value within 1.5 × IQR - Red dots: outliers beyond 1.5 × IQR (1 in Control, 2 in Intervention; the lowest BMI is 11.4)
OBSERVATION: - Median BMI 24.6 (Control) and 25.8 (Intervention) - Intervention box slightly taller (IQR 6.3 vs 5.4): a little more spread - Boxes largely overlap - A few very low BMI values appear as outliers
INTERPRETATION: - A difference of about 1 BMI unit between the groups at baseline; small next to the spread within each group - The groups look broadly comparable on BMI - The very low values (below 15) are implausible and should be checked
IMPLICATIONS: - A baseline difference this small is unlikely to confound a treatment comparison, but it can be adjusted for - Report the medians and IQRs in Table 1 - Decide what to do with implausible values before the analysis, and say so in the methods

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Understanding Box Plots


The Box: - Bottom edge: Q1 (25th percentile) - Middle line: Median (50th percentile) - Top edge: Q3 (75th percentile) - Box height: IQR (Q3 - Q1)
The Whiskers: - Extend to 1.5 × IQR - Show data range (excluding outliers)

Outliers: - Points beyond whiskers - May indicate: - Data entry errors - Natural extreme values - Different population
Comparing Boxes: - Non-overlapping: likely different - Overlapping: may not be different - Check median positions - Compare IQR widths

title: Category vs. Continuous - BASIC
text:
Key Takeaways

Remember:

Box plots show distribution - not just means
Order categories - by median or logically
Grouped vs. Stacked bars - different purposes
Always show units - in axis labels
Handle outliers thoughtfully - investigate but don’t automatically remove

Common Mistakes:

Too many categories in one plot (>8)
Not ordering categories logically
Confusing grouped and stacked bars
Ignoring outliers without investigation
Comparing means without showing variation

text:
How to Read Bar Charts
Using the previous plot as example:

OBSERVATION: - Non-smokers: 118 patients (largest group) - Former smokers: 43 patients - Current smokers: 37 patients (smallest group) - Clear ranking, with no group very small
INTERPRETATION: - 60% of participants are non-smokers - Current and former smokers together are 40% - Every smoking group has enough patients to describe
IMPLICATIONS: - Subgroups of smokers are still small (37 and 43): estimates within them will be imprecise - Non-smokers carry most of the weight of overall results - Consider stratified analysis by smoking status
ACTIONS: - Use smoking status as a stratification variable - Check statistical power before testing smoker subgroups - Watch for interaction effects with treatment

🔴 Goal: Part of a Whole

treatment_summary <- data_clean %>%
  count(TreatmentGroup) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100)  # Calculate percentages

# Create pie chart using coord_polar transformation

  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1, color = "white") +  # Create stacked bar
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +  # Transform to polar coordinates (pie)
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Control" = "#E74C3C", "Intervention" = "#3498DB")) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(percentage, 1), "%")), 
            position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5),
            family = "serif", size = 5) +  # Add percentage labels

       fill = "Group") +
  theme_void(base_family = "serif") +  # Remove axes for clean pie

text:
🗓️ Self-study plan
Work through the steps in order. Every page ends with a self-check quiz, and each step has a lab (an R script with blanks to fill in; it reads the NCD survey). Keep the Basic cheat sheet open. Tick a step when you have finished it; ticks are saved in this browser.


Set up R and write your first lines

Wrangle a dataset

Draw your first plots
Grammar of Graphics, then copy and adapt examples from the Basic Plot Gallery. Lab: b4_first_plots.R.
Choose and run a statistical test
Test Selection Guide, then ggstatsplot — Intro to plot a test and its result together. Lab: b5_which_test.R.
Meet regression
Regression Analysis: a first look. The Regression track covers it in depth.
Write it up
Quarto Basics: turn your code and results into a report. Lab: b6_first_report.R.
Check yourself and move on
Take the Region 1 post-test in the game. At 70% or more, continue with the Moderate track (Step 2 on the main page).

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

ggbetweenstats() — Group Comparisons
Use this when you want to compare a continuous variable across two or more independent groups.

library(ggstatsplot)

# Compare systolic BP across physical-activity groups
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = ncd,
  x     = phys_act,         # grouping variable (categorical)
  y     = sbp,            # outcome variable (continuous)
  title = "Systolic BP by Physical Activity"
)








What the output shows:

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = ncd,
  x     = phys_act,
  y     = sbp,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

How to Read Histograms
Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Ages range from 18 to 79 years (median 50) - Patients are spread over the whole range, with somewhat more between 45 and 55 - No single sharp peak and no long tail - No gaps and no impossible values
INTERPRETATION: - The study covers the whole adult age range - No age group dominates the sample - Age is not normally distributed, but that does not matter for using it as a predictor

Using the previous plot:

OBSERVATION: - Baseline (Month 0): mean systolic BP 135.1 mmHg - Month 3: 132.2 mmHg (2.9 mmHg lower) - Month 6: 130.4 mmHg (another 1.8 mmHg lower) - Steady downward trend, no rebound

ACTIONS: - Always show a line per group in a trial - Add error bars or confidence intervals before drawing conclusions

Key Time Series Concepts


Trend: - Overall direction (up, down, flat) - Long-term pattern - Calculate: moving average, regression
Seasonality: - Regular periodic fluctuations - Daily, weekly, monthly patterns - Example: Higher BP in winter
Volatility: - Amount of variation - High = unstable, Low = stable - Measure: standard deviation

Data Preparation: - Wide format: One column per time point - Long format: One row per observation - Use pivot_longer() to convert
Best Practices: - Always show all time points - Use consistent time intervals - Label axes clearly with units - Consider adding reference lines - Show confidence intervals when relevant

title: Time Series - BASIC

Connect the dots - use geom_line() to show continuity
Add points - helps identify exact time points
Multiple lines need legends - make groups clear
Show uncertainty - confidence intervals add credibility
Wide to long format - essential for time series plotting

Common Mistakes:

Not connecting points (scatter instead of line)
Too many lines (>5 becomes cluttered)
Inconsistent time intervals without noting
Missing baseline comparisons
Not handling missing time points
